items.text: Heat plus the 40% off Ice Break Iced Coffee 500mL promotion: plan 595 cases for National Retailer A on Wed 14 Oct, not 397.
Nambour line 3 is over capacity on Thu 15 Oct and Fri 16 Oct. Make 562 cases earlier on spare time; no overtime needed.
Milk silos run about 3,143 L short on Fri 16 Oct. Moving one white-milk run to Sat 17 Oct fixes it at no extra cost.

also.text: Today's method under-calls Mon 12 Oct because it copies the King's Birthday holiday
Cut Ice Break Iced Coffee 750mL, Oak Iced Coffee 600mL, Breaka Iced Coffee 750mL, Ice Break Iced Coffee Less Sugar 500mL at National Retailer A during the promotion

qa.question: Why is the Ice Break Iced Coffee 500mL forecast so high on Wed 14 Oct?
qa.answer: Three things add up. A normal Wednesday at National Retailer A is 321 cases. The 40% off promotion adds 206. The 34°C heat (normal is 26°C) adds 68. Total 595 cases, likely range 420 to 792. Today's method says 397 because it only copies last week.

qa.question: What if it is only 28°C on Wed 14 Oct?
qa.answer: At {temp}°C with the promotion, all customers together need about {iced} cases of iced coffee on Wed 14 Oct, and {hero} cases of Ice Break Iced Coffee 500mL. At the forecast 34°C it is 4,532 and 2,086.

qa.question: What if the promotion is 25% off instead of 40%?
qa.answer: At {depth}% off, National Retailer A needs about {hero_c} cases of Ice Break Iced Coffee 500mL on Wed 14 Oct (595 at 40% off, {none} with no promotion). Iced coffee across all customers: {iced} cases. The size of the lift is learned from 263 past promotions.

qa.question: How accurate is the forecast?
qa.answer: We replayed 2026-01-01 to 2026-10-11 day by day, forecasting 14 days ahead with forecast (not actual) weather. Today's method was 74.2% accurate; the AI was 84.0%. That is 38% less error. This is synthetic data: on real data we would aim for at least 20% less error in the pilot.

qa.question: Where does the AI help most?
qa.answer: Biggest gains: public holidays and the day before 87% to 20% error; products next to a promotion 34% to 16% error; school holidays 31% to 15% error; all days 26% to 16% error. These are the days when copying last week goes wrong.

qa.question: Why does today's method get Mon 12 Oct wrong?
qa.answer: It copies last Mon 5 Oct, which was the King's Birthday public holiday, so it plans only 129 cases of Ice Break Iced Coffee 500mL for National Retailer A. The AI knows it was a holiday and forecasts 413. In the back-test, holidays and the day before had 87% error with today's method and 20% with the AI.

qa.question: Which products lose sales because of the promotion?
qa.answer: Shoppers switch to the discounted Ice Break Iced Coffee 500mL at National Retailer A. Over the promotion week: Ice Break Iced Coffee 750mL: 311 fewer cases over the week; Oak Iced Coffee 600mL: 170 fewer cases over the week; Breaka Iced Coffee 750mL: 160 fewer cases over the week; Ice Break Iced Coffee Less Sugar 500mL: 120 fewer cases over the week. Today's method would plan 258 cases too many, about A$2,873 at cost at risk of write-off.

qa.question: Can Nambour make enough this week?
qa.answer: Lines 1 and 2 are fine. Line 3 (flavoured milk and iced coffee) is over on Thu 15 Oct (104%) and Fri 16 Oct (104%), 562 cases in total. It has 1,975 spare cases before that, so making them earlier avoids overtime. An extra shift adds up to 2,000 cases a day if needed.

qa.question: Do we have enough raw milk?
qa.answer: Not quite. Hot days cut farm intake by about 3%, and demand peaks at the same time. The silos end Fri 16 Oct about 3,143 L short. Moving 300 cases of Pauls Full Cream Milk 2L to Sat 17 Oct, when intake recovers and line 1 has room, leaves about 2,257 L. Buying about 5,000 L of spot milk is the back-up. Note: the silo starting level is an assumption.

qa.question: How much could this save?
qa.answer: We replayed 2026-01-01 to 2026-10-11 (284 days) through the same stock rules, changing only the forecast. Write-offs fell from 1.63% to 1.04% of production (36% fewer) and orders filled rose from 98.73% to 99.84%. On this synthetic Queensland range that is about A$339k a year and 324,757 L of milk not wasted. Real gains will be smaller; the pilot target is at least 15% fewer write-offs.

qa.question: Which orders still use old Fonterra codes?
qa.answer: Since 1 Apr 2026 some National Retailer B and Independent Grocers orders arrive under old Fonterra codes (FON-QLD-0412, FON-QLD-0877). The share fell from 17% in April to 7% in the last 4 weeks (858 order lines). 8 orders were keyed in twice (old and new code) and came back as 273 cases of returns.

qa.question: How many Fonterra customers match our records?
qa.answer: We compared 127 Fonterra customer records with 183 Lactalis ones. 69 matched automatically (100.0% correct when checked against the answer key), 2 need a person to check, and 56 look like new customers. Overall 98.6% of the real pairs were found.

qa.question: Are there price conflicts?
qa.answer: Yes. 9 products have an old Fonterra price for National Retailer B that differs from the Lactalis list by -6% to +4%. The largest gap is Breaka Iced Coffee 750mL. The agent flags these for the commercial team; it does not change prices.

qa.question: What are we throwing away today?
qa.answer: In the last 12 months (synthetic): short-dated / expired in DC 89,394 cases; damaged in handling 1,999 cases; customer return: duplicate order under legacy Fonterra code 273 cases. Most short-dated stock is Pauls Full Cream Milk 2L, Pauls Reduced Fat Milk 2L, Pauls Full Cream Milk 3L.

qa.question: What data does the model use?
qa.answer: Order history by product, customer and day, plus three outside signals: the weather forecast, school and public holidays, and the promotion calendar (including promotions on neighbouring products). The model is LightGBM (Poisson), SKU x customer x day. Each signal was tested on and off: for iced coffee the error went from 26.0% with history only to 16.4% with all three.

qa.question: Who decides? Does the AI change the plan by itself?
qa.answer: No. Agents suggest; a planner approves or rejects every change, and each decision is written to the audit log with the reason. Rules such as minimum shelf life, line capacity and price lists are never changed by an agent.

qa.question: Is this real Lactalis data?
qa.answer: No. The data is synthetic, built to look like a Queensland fresh milk range after the Fonterra purchase and the South Brisbane closure. The forecast model is real and was trained on that data. Agent answers in this demo are pre-configured; in a pilot they would come from a live AI model reading your data.

qa.question: What would a pilot look like?
qa.answer: Start with one region and the fresh milk and iced coffee range. Connect order history, the promotion calendar, weather and plant data; run the forecast next to today's method; let planners approve agent suggestions. Pilot targets: at least 20% less forecast error and at least 15% fewer write-offs, measured on real data.

qa.question: Which days are hot this week?
qa.answer: Forecast maximums in Brisbane: Mon 12 Oct 28°C, Tue 13 Oct 30°C, Wed 14 Oct 34°C, Thu 15 Oct 35°C, Fri 16 Oct 33°C, Sat 17 Oct 29°C, Sun 18 Oct 27°C. Days over 32°C: Wed 14 Oct, Thu 15 Oct, Fri 16 Oct. On hot days the AI had 16% error vs 23% for today's method.

qa.question: What is the total forecast for the promotion week?
qa.answer: For Ice Break Iced Coffee 500mL at National Retailer A, Wed 14 Oct to Tue 20 Oct: 4,145 cases (AI) vs 2,386 (today's method). Across all products and customers the AI forecasts 101,356 cases that week.

qa.question: What does the label check look for?
qa.answer: Allergens in bold and in the 'Contains' statement, nutrition claims against their conditions (for example 'good source of protein' needs 10 g per serve), the Health Star Rating graphic against the nutrition panel and the current recipe, per-serve arithmetic, origin wording, and 'fresh' wording on milk with reconstituted ingredients. The cartons here are a fictional brand.

qa.question: Does the label agent approve artwork by itself?
qa.answer: No. It finds and explains issues; the regulatory reviewer sends each one to the team that owns the fix (food safety, marketing, nutrition, legal, procurement) or marks it not an issue, and every decision is logged. It makes the check faster and more consistent; it does not replace sign-off.

qa.question: How does this connect to SAP?
qa.answer: In this demo the SAP step is simulated: each approval shows the change it would send. In a pilot the agents start read-only, using extracts of orders, the material and customer masters and the production plan. Writing approved changes back uses standard SAP interfaces agreed with your IT and security teams, and only after a person approves.

qa.question: What would you need from Lactalis?
qa.answer: About two years of orders by product, customer and day; the promotion calendar; plant line capacities and the production plan; milk intake; write-offs; and both customer lists. Plus a few hours a week from a demand planner and a supply planner to review suggestions, and read-only data access agreed with IT.

qa.question: Can it cover other regions and products?
qa.answer: Yes. The same approach runs per region and per product range. The pilot starts with Queensland fresh milk and iced coffee because short shelf life makes errors costly. Other regions are added once accuracy is proven on real data; longer-life ranges such as cheese and yoghurt use the same models with their own shelf-life rules.

qa.question: Is our data safe?
qa.answer: In a pilot the data stays in an environment your IT security team approves, with role-based access and every action logged. Your data is not used to train public AI models. The exact set-up is agreed with your IT team before any data moves.

qa.question: What does the pilot cost?
qa.answer: The commercial proposal covers that separately. The pilot is fixed in scope and time, and its value is measured against today's method on your own data before any wider roll-out.

qa.question: Why this forecasting model?
qa.answer: LightGBM is proven for demand forecasting at this scale: it handles thousands of product, customer and day combinations, retrains daily in minutes and shows which signals drove each number. Language models are used to explain results in plain words, not to produce the numbers.
